meta.title: Who really said "Glory is fleeting, but obscurity is forever"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Everyone credits Napoleon — but no letter, speech, or French original exists. Wikiquote removed it as unsourced. An apocryphal aphorism, not a documented quote.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Glory is fleeting, but obscurity is forever'?
meta.ogDescription: Pinned on Napoleon everywhere, sourced nowhere. No primary text, no French original, removed from Wikiquote as unsourced — the marks of a modern apocryphal line.

answer.label: Not documented from Napoleon — an unsourced modern aphorism
answer.authorDates: 1769–1821 · Emperor of the French, military commander
answer.sourceLine: Universally pinned on Napoleon across quote sites, yet no letter, speech, memoir, or French original has ever been produced for it. Wikiquote removed it as unsourced, Quote Investigator has never written it up, and its crisp English antithesis reads far more like a 20th-century aphorism than anything in Napoleon’s documented words.

source.heading: The paper trail (or lack of one)

docMeta.dd: None located — no letter, speech, memoir, or French original

source.excerpt: Glory is fleeting, but obscurity is forever.
trail: Every major quote database — BrainyQuote and Goodreads among them — credits Napoleon by name only, with no book, speech, or letter attached; Goodreads even flags that its quotes are “not verified.”
Wikiquote does not carry the line in its sourced or attributed sections; its Talk:Napoleon page files it under “Unsourced quotes removed” — struck for want of any citation.
Quote Investigator, which has traced hundreds of Napoleon attributions, has never published an entry on this one — there is no attested chain of sources to trace.

No French text (« La gloire est éphémère… » or similar) surfaces in any edition of Napoleon’s correspondence or the memoirs of Las Cases, Gourgaud, or Montholon — a telling absence for a supposedly Napoleonic maxim.
source.excerptNote: The line as it circulates — always in polished English, never with a French original such as one would expect from a genuine Napoleonic saying.
source.rightsNote: Because no source work or first-publication can be identified — the wording appears to be a modern English aphorism of unknown authorship — no copyright status can honestly be asserted. It is neither demonstrably public-domain nor tied to an identifiable rights-holder.

author.name: Napoleon Bonaparte
author.heading: About the man it’s pinned on
author.metaLine: 1769–1821 · Emperor of the French, military commander
author.bio: Napoleon Bonaparte rose from Corsican artillery officer to Emperor of the French, reshaping Europe through the Napoleonic Wars before his defeat at Waterloo and exile on St. Helena. He left a vast documented record — correspondence, decrees, and the St. Helena memoirs dictated to companions like the Comte de Las Cases — which is exactly why the absence of this line from his papers is meaningful. Many worldly aphorisms are attached to his name; only some are genuinely his.

cite.sourceCitation: No documented source. Earliest instances are late-20th- and 21st-century quotation databases and blogs attributing the line to Napoleon Bonaparte with no primary citation; removed from Wikiquote’s Napoleon article as unsourced.
cite.pageCitation: Quotle.info. “Who really said ‘Glory is fleeting, but obscurity is forever’?” Last verified 16 Jul 2026.

misattribution.heading: How Napoleon got the credit
misattribution.intro: Napoleon is one of the internet’s great quote magnets: pithy, worldly-wise lines drift toward his name because it lends them instant gravitas. This is one of them — repeated endlessly, sourced never.

items.why: Quote sites, merch, and social posts credit him by name with no citation. Goodreads attaches only the name and warns its quotes are community-added and “not verified.”

items.who: “Fame is fleeting, but obscurity is forever” — sometimes tossed to Napoleon Hill
items.why: A variant swaps “glory” for “fame” and, in at least one social post, lands on Napoleon Hill — a slip between the two Napoleons that underlines how loosely the line is sourced.

misattribution.truthLine: No primary text supports it. The safest statement is that it is an apocryphal aphorism attached to Napoleon’s name — struck from Wikiquote for exactly that reason.

context.heading: Why it sticks to him
lead: The sentiment is real enough to feel Napoleonic — a soldier’s bleak arithmetic that fame fades while the void of being forgotten does not. That resonance is precisely why the line migrates to Napoleon rather than staying anonymous: the name supplies a backstory the words themselves lack.

But resonance is not evidence. Napoleon left one of history’s most thoroughly documented paper trails — tens of thousands of letters, plus the St. Helena memoirs of Las Cases and others. A maxim this quotable would leave a footprint in that record if it were his. It doesn’t.
context.pull: Pinned on Napoleon everywhere, sourced nowhere.
